2720.dq: The stress regime in Mono-Alu operates on the level of the prosodic word. Affixation and cliticisation do not affect the regularity of the stress regime. Stress shifts to apply regularly to the larger prosodic domain that results from affixation and cliticisation. ... In imperative clauses, clause level stress overrides stress assignment on the word level. (p. 74)
2720.dloc: Ch. 2 'Phonology', sec. 2.4 'Stress', pp. 74-85; rule statement sec. 2.4.2 'Regular stress assignment', pp. 75-77; Tables 2.15-2.20 pp. 76-78; 5-7 mora roots p. 78; domain statement pp. 74-75; stress cues sec. 2.4.1 p. 75; affixes/clitics sec. 2.4.3 pp. 80-82; reduplication sec. 2.4.4 pp. 82-84; imperative override sec. 2.4.5 pp. 84-85 and sec. 5.13.3 pp. 534-535; ch. 1 summary sec. 1.2.1 p. 9; vowel length and weight sec. 2.1.1.7 'Length' pp. 39-43.
2720.heavy: Bimoraic syllables: the syllable structure is (C)V(V)(N), 'as only nasals can occupy the coda position' (sec. 1.2.1, p. 9). Table 2.20 (p. 78) treats (C)VV (diphthong) and (C)VN as heavy: /'Pau.Pau/ 'dog', /'bun.nao/ 'big squid', /'siN.ka.pe/ 'green fly', /'tau.Pi.Pi/ 'child', /i.'Ran.Ran/ 'cicada'; haulu /'hau.lu/ is a diphthong case ('The first two vowels in the root form a diphthong', p. 80). Underlyingly long vowels /a:, o:, u: also make a syllable heavy (sec. 2.1.1.7, pp. 39-43: ava=Pang [a'va:PaN] 'because the long vowel in the second syllable renders it heavy', p. 40; ta-hata [ta'ha:ta] 'as this syllable is heavy due to the long vowel', p. 42; hata 'analysed as having a first heavy syllable, due to an underlyingly long vowel /a:/', p. 85; /'Ri:.la/, /'to:.la/, /'ka:.pa/ Table 2.29, p. 84).
2720.dflt: Initial stress in words of 2 or 3 light syllables ('pa.tu, 'ka.pe.Re); second syllable (= antepenult) in four light syllables (ma.'ta.la.e, ta.'he.so.lo); antepenultimate mora in 5-6 light-mora words (ma.ta.'pu.li.si,ko.a.'ko.a.pa, ha.,ma.li.'lu.a.na).
2720.prule: Word-final syllable is extrametrical regardless of weight; the remaining morae are parsed right-to-left into moraic trochees (heavy = bimoraic syllable: (C)VV diphthong or underlying long vowel, or (C)VN, N being the only permitted coda); primary stress on the first mora of the rightmost (final) foot. Outcomes given by the source: 2- and 3-mora words initial ('pa.tu, 'ka.pe.Re, 'pao.Pa, 'pa.pau); four light syllables -> second syllable = antepenult (ma.'ta.la.e, ta.'he.so.lo); heavy penult attracts stress (i.'Ran.Ran); heavy initial + light penult -> initial ('tau.Pi.Pi, 'siN.ka.pe); 5-7 mora words -> antepenultimate mora with secondary stress on the first mora of the preceding (penultimate) foot (ma.ta.'pu.li.si, ha.,ma.li.'lu.a.na, ka.,kun.tu.'nu.ga.la); heavy final syllable is still extrametrical (ta.'Ra.ko.hou).
2720.srule: Secondary stress on the first mora of the penultimate foot, i.e. the moraic trochee immediately to the left of the primary-stress foot (final syllable extrametrical): /,ma.ta.'pu.li.si/ 'eyelash', /,ko.a.'ko.a.pa/ 'fair skinned', /ha.,ma.li.'lu.a.na/ 'bless', /,mo.Ro.'kaN.ka.ga/ 'taro species', /ka.,kun.tu.'nu.ga.la/ 'yellow bamboo' (p. 78); likewise in suffixed and encliticised words, /,tan.'na.Ri.a/, /a.,la.pa.'tu.Ri.a/ (Table 2.22, p. 81), /,tau.Pi.'Pi.a.PaN/ (Table 2.24, p. 82). Only one secondary (the penultimate foot) is stated; no longer words are given.

2721.tone: Source says nothing about stress or accent: a full-text search over the whole paper gives 'stress' 0, 'accent' 0 (the one 'prominent' is p. 79 n. 4 on a glottal stop being 'not very prominent'). What it does say: 'Monsang is a tone language' with two lexical tones H and L on the syllable as TBU, minimal pairs in table 5 (e.g. sá 'meat' vs sà 'eat', í:n 'house' vs ì:n 'drink'), both tones fall slightly at the end of the f0 track, vowel length is independent of tone, some words (e.g. in 'curry') are 'toneless', and 'there are pitch contrasts only in limited words'; polysyllabic and phrasal tone/prosody left for future work. Konnerth 2018 (HL 17(1), sec. 1.4) agrees: 'Monsang has a low and a high tone, which are generally a property of the syllable. Both tones occur in every syllable type.' Konnerth 2018 n. 8 and Konnerth & Wanglar 2019 p. 54: bare verb stems are neutralised to low tone, underlying tone surfaces under prefixation (í-bìn 'NMLZ-beat' L vs í-sí 'NMLZ-go' H). 2723.dq: The comment about lengthening when words are said in isolation suggests that if there is lengthening, it may be due to a word produced by itself in isolation or at the end of an utterance, rather than word internal stress, so called 'phrase-final lengthening'.
2723.dloc: Grammar sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress', pp. 47-48; tone system Ch. 4, p. 95. NLLT 2011: pp. 228, 234, 246.
2723.heavy: Not applicable to the record. In the carried Black & Black rule a closed final syllable attracts stress ('If the last syllable is closed, it is stressed'), i.e. CVC-heavy at the right edge, with an additional segmental /ə/-avoidance clause.
2723.prule: No word-stress rule. Moro is a two-tone language (H vs L; H spreads/shifts/downsteps, L inert, analysed as privative H vs zero). The reference grammar finds that tone is not a correlate of stress (any syllable type and any vowel may bear H or L), that a small duration study shows no systematic positional lengthening, and it explicitly leaves the existence of stress or any non-tonal prominence undetermined.

tn.quote: Moro contrasts two tones, high (H) and low (L). ... High tone is marked with an accent ́, whereas low tone is unmarked. ... High tone can spread, shift and trigger downstep in the case of adjacent H tones, whereas low tone is inert: it does not spread, shift, or trigger phonological processes. Additionally, there are no lexically contrastive contour tones in Moro (e.g. Section 4.6.1). These are all properties of languages for which a H vs. ∅ tone contrast has been proposed (Hyman 2006); see also Jenks & Rose (2011) for further discussion.

2724.dq: stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. [...] When any suffix or enclitic is added, the stress normally shifts, staying on the penultimate syllable of the word. This contrasts with many Sulawesi languages in which enclitics are extrametrical, causing no shift of stress. (p.10)
2724.dloc: Sec. 4 'Syllabification and stress' pp.10-15: sec. 4.1 'Basic Pattern' p.10 (basic statement, Chart 3, shift under suffix/enclitic); variation under enclitics p.11 set (B); sec. 4.3 'Geminate Vowels' pp.11-12 (sets C-D, Muthalib et al. 1991:25 'penultimate except for final long vowels'); sec. 4.4 'Diphthongization' p.12 (sets E-I, 'stress is not always on the penultimate syllable'); sec. 4.5 'Syllabification and Stress Rules' p.13 (formal rules; /βu.ˈɽaa.u/, /ˈdaa.u/); worked derivation p.14; sec. 4.6 'Secondary stress' pp.14-15.
2724.heavy: Not stated in weight vocabulary (no 'heavy', no 'quantity'; 'dimoraic' occurs once, p.14, of reduplication, not of stress). Operationally: syllabification rules 2-3 (p.13) make a geminate VV or an /aV/, /ei/, /oi/, /ou/ sequence the two-vowel nucleus of one syllable, and stress rule 1 targets 'the syllable dominating the penultimate vowel of word', so a word-final two-vowel syllable takes the stress ([tuˈaⁱ] 'younger sibling', [moˈgaᵘ] 'speak', [ʔoˈpaː] 'four'; /ˈdaa.u/ 'your being' stressed on the geminate) = CVV heavy; a word-final single vowel never does. No CVC: 'There are no words ending in a consonant' and prenasalized stops are single onsets (p.11). The author cites Muthalib et al. 1991:25 as analysing stress 'penultimate except for final long vowels' and prefers the geminate analysis because it 'preserves the penultimate stress pattern' (p.12), i.e. penultimate by vowel count.
2724.prule: Primary stress on the syllable containing the penultimate VOWEL of the phonological word (suffixes and enclitics inside the domain, so stress shifts rightward under affixation/cliticization). Under the source's own syllabification (p.13 rules 2-3) a geminate VV or an /aV/, /ei/, /oi/, /ou/ sequence is the two-vowel nucleus of ONE syllable, so by syllable the pattern is: stress the final syllable if its nucleus has two vowels ([tuˈaⁱ] 'younger sibling', [moˈgaᵘ] 'speak', [ʔoˈpaː] 'four'), otherwise the penult ([ˈki.re] 'eyebrow', [βo.ˈtu.tu] 'mosquito net', [ˈkiː.ri] 'shave'); within a two-vowel syllable the first vowel carries the stress (/ˈkiiri/, [ˈkoⁱe] 'that', [paˈŋaᵘβa] 'sail', /ˈdaa.u/ 'your being'). Equivalent to a penultimate-mora rule with CVV heavy (there are no codas; prenasalized stops are single onsets, p.11). The author frames it as penultimate-vowel stress and never as weight; he reports the competing analysis (Muthalib et al. 1991:25) as 'penultimate except for final long vowels' and states 'stress is not always on the penultimate syllable' (p.12). Stress is non-contrastive.
2724.srule: Two rules (Andersen 1999 sec. 4.6). (1) Alternating: in four- and five-syllable words the fourth-from-last syllable (two syllables left of the penultimate primary) takes secondary stress: [ˌkiniˈβia] 'afternoon', [poˌpateˈaku] 'kill me'. (2) Demarcative, in words of more than five syllables: every subunit of two or more syllables (prefix cluster, stem, reduplicant) takes secondary stress on its own penult ([ˌmopo-ˌpate-ˈaku] 'to kill me'); where the two conflict the demarcative rule wins; a morpheme's penultimate stress is suppressed when the primary falls on its final syllable. Monosyllabic prefixes are generally unstressed; nominative proclitics always carry secondary stress; two stems (/sumiarara/, /ʔoŋkona/) are lexically marked for initial secondary stress, so secondary stress is 'not entirely predictable' (p.15).

2725.tone: Sec. 2a 'Tone' (1966 print pp. 30-31; reprint PT37, same image as the stress passage): 'Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In the MORU-MA'DI languages so far investigated (MORU, MA'DI, LOGO, LUGBARA) and in LENDU, three tone levels have been established, and the same would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE.'... 'In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs.'. Moru is thus a three-level tone language for which the same source states an explicit initial word-stress rule; tone or pitch accent (defined as no stress rule) does not apply. The stress statement is Tucker's own impressionistic field observation on Moru Miza (comparative table on the same page headed 'MORU (MIZA)'). Kilpatrick 2004 (OPSL 9: 88, 'All Moru-Madi languages have three level tones') and Tucker 1940 (scan search-inside, lending-locked) describe the three tones and state no Moru stress rule.

2729.tone: Two tones H and L, but 'no phonological tone is distinguished in nouns and verbs' (H. Kröger 2026 p. 53); 'Untypisch für Bantu weist das Ngoni weder lexikalischen noch grammatischen Ton auf' (O. Kröger 2015 p. 3). Every word in isolation carries LH...L (disyllables HL), high through the penult and low on the final; the drop is phrase-final, not word-final (§5.1.2: 'the lowering of the tone melody at the end of the word takes place not word but phrase finally'); low-toned prefixes (ka-, object prefixes) delay the rise, future ti- starts H; the penult H may surface as a HL fall (fn. 52); sentential downdrift is terraced by constituent (§5.1.4). The tone melody is thus a demarcative (ordinative) accent that coincides with the penult intensity peak; the 2015 source treats tone + intensity + phrase-final penult length together as 'Akzent'. The 2026 grammar never uses the word 'stress' but marks accent on the penult of adapted Portuguese loans (mɛ.ˈtu.lu < metro, ka.dɛ.ˈlu.nu < caderno, p. 49: the epenthesis 'shifts the accent in relation to the Portuguese word which continues on the penult').

2730.dq: There is typically one accent per lexical item, realised as high tone . [...] accent on verbs typically falls on the first syllable of the stem (demarcated by -), whether the verb occurs in infinitival form or is conjugated .
2730.dloc: Sec. 2.11 'Accent', p. 697 ('one accent per lexical item') and sec. 2.11.2 'Accent in verbs', p. 698
2730.prule: One culminative accent per lexical item, realised as high tone (author undecided whether pitch-accent or stress-accent; vowel centralisation around the accent suggests stress). Position is morphologically anchored: the first syllable of the STEM in nouns (di-/trisyllabic stems) and in verbs (infinitive or conjugated), noun-class and verbal prefixes being unaccented; not computable from word syllable count.
2730.srule: None: 'There is typically one accent per lexical item, realised as high tone' - the accent is culminative and secs. 2.11-2.11.2 (pp. 697-698) place that single accent only; no secondary or rhythmic accent is discussed (text seen as excerpt windows).
2730.quote: 2.11 Accent There is typically one accent per lexical item, realised as high tone . However, it is not clear whether accent here is best described as pitch - accent or stress - accent . tn.quote: Chaque syllabe, en mulwi, est affectée d'un ton. L'analyse permet de dégager deux registres tonals (Haut) et (Bas) par rapport auxquels se situent quatre tonèmes (ou tons): ... Haut ... Bas ... Descendant ... Montant Il n'y aurait pas d'inconvénient à analyser les deux tonèmes modulés en une succession de deux mores: Haut + Bas = Descendant Bas + Haut = Montant. ... Le rendement distinctif des oppositions tonales n'est pas très important dans le lexique. Il est par contre très fort en grammaire ... l'opposition Haut / Bas est la marque de l'opposition "inaccompli" / "accompli".
tn.translation: Every syllable in Mulwi is assigned a tone. The analysis yields two tonal registers (High) and (Low), relative to which four tonemes (or tones) are placed: High, Low, Falling, Rising. There would be no drawback in analysing the two modulated tonemes as a succession of two moras: High + Low = Falling, Low + High = Rising. ... The distinctive yield of the tonal oppositions is not very great in the lexicon. It is on the other hand very strong in the grammar ... the High / Low opposition is the mark of the 'imperfective' / 'perfective' opposition.
tn.cite: Tourneux, Henry. 1978. Le mulwi de Mogroum (Tchad): phonologie, éléments de grammaire. Thèse de 3e cycle, Univ. de la Sorbonne Nouvelle (Paris III). 325 pp. HAL tel-02372418.
tn.locator: ch. 3 Tonématique §3.1, thesis p. 34; §3.27, thesis p. 48
tn.note: Two registers (Haut, Bas), four tonemes; the falling and rising tonemes are said to be analysable as H+B / B+H over two moras. Lexical load of tone is low; aspect is marked by H vs B.

2736.cfw: Tourneux 1978, the only modern first-hand description, gives every Mulwi syllable one of four tonemes on two registers with lexical minimal pairs and never mentions stress, and Tourneux 1991 calls the Cameroon Munjuk of Pouss a tone language too, so the sole contrary statement, a tendency to stress the final syllable of isolated nouns and adjectives in Krause's 1880s travel notes edited by Müller 1886, is an untrained pre-phonemic report that the modern grammar outweighs.

2737.heavy: Not framed as weight by the authors: the sole condition is the vowel quality of the penult -- a penult whose vowel is the schwa /e/ ('bunyi vokal pepet /e/') cannot carry the stress, which moves to the ultima; any penult with a full vowel is stressed. 2737.dflt: Ultima, by the letter of the rule: the shift to the final syllable is conditioned only on the penult having schwa ('bila suku kedua dari suku terakhir itu mempunyai bunyi vokal pepet /e/'), with no condition on the ultima's vowel. 2737.prule: Stress is predictable (non-phonemic). A stressed word-final vowel is phonetically somewhat long ([retí:], [semelé:], [peró:], [pedú:], sec. 3.5.2).

Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. [...] With the exception of the utterance-final increase, stress in general may not prove to be a significant factor in Muyang. However, further research is needed before the possible existence of word…
2739.dloc: Ch. 5 'Stress', sections 5.1-5.3, p.30; tone system Ch. 4 'Tone' section 4.1, p.27.
2739.prule: No word-level stress rule is stated. Muyang is described as a tone language (three level surface tones H/M/L, possibly two underlying). The only firm prominence statement is utterance-level: the final syllable of an utterance receives relatively great stress (amplitude, and always length, about doubling the final syllable), which masks any word pattern in isolation forms. Within nouns amplitude correlates with high tone; the author says that if word-level stress exists at all it is closely tied to tone, and concludes that apart from the utterance-final increase stress 'may not prove to be a significant factor', with word-level stress left open pending further research.
2739.srule: Not mentioned in Smith 1999 (Ch. 5 'Stress' §§5.1-5.3, p.30; Ch. 8 'Conclusion', p.52; full text consulted): the source treats only utterance-final prominence and the tone-amplitude link and leaves even word-level stress undetermined.

Normal Muyang speech applies relatively great stress to the final syllable of an utterance. This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length – almost equivalent to doubling the length of the vocalisation of a final syllable. Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. ... Amplitude and high tone in Muyang are linked. In nouns of three syllables there is a fairly consistent correlat…
2739.loc: Ch. 5 'Stress', sections 5.1-5.3, p.30; tone system Ch. 4 'Tone' section 4.1, p.27.

2739.exq_: Nouns of two syllables starting with high tone have a tendency to break the link between tone and amplitude, suggesting that there may be an overriding tendency towards word-final stress in disyllabic nouns.
2739.tone: Ch. 4 section 4.1 (p.27): 'Muyang has three level surface tones, high (H), mid (M) and low (L). There are a certain number of pairs of words which are distinguished minimally by tone, e.g. [àxár] (LH) "arm, hand" [àxàr] (LL) "head" [áxàr] (HL) "he/she winnows"'; 'Given the existence of depressor consonants and the general lack of three-way contrast, it may prove after further analysis that at an underlying level there are only two tones, high and low.' Section 4.2.1: 'Verb roots in Muyang do not as a rule carry lexical tone. Tense/aspect forms carry tone melodies that blanket the word suprasegmentally in the same way that prosodies do.' On stress vs tone (p.30): amplitude and high tone are linked in nouns; 'if stress is relevant at word-level at all, it is closely linked to tone'; no independent word-stress rule is given, and the author explicitly leaves word-level stress undetermined.

tn.quote: Avant de dégager les tonèmes proprement dits, nous nous proposons de faire la liste des différentes hauteurs de la voix (ou tons) attestées dans la langue. L’orungu présente des tons dits ponctuels et des tons modulés. Au nombre de trois, les tons ponctuels sont: 1- Le ton haut, désigné par H et noté par un accent aigu . … 2- Le ton bas, désigné par B et noté par un accent grave . … 3- Le ton haut-abaissé caractérisant un niveau intermédiaire entre le ton haut et le ton bas, désigné par A et noté par un trait vertical (/). … Les tons modulés sont d’une extrême rareté en orungu.
tn.translation: Before isolating the tonemes proper, we list the different voice pitches (or tones) attested in the language. Orungu has so-called level (punctual) tones and modulated (contour) tones. Three in number, the level tones are: 1- the high tone, designated H and written with an acute accent. … 2- the low tone, designated B and written with a grave accent. … 3- the lowered-high (haut-abaissé) tone, characterising a level intermediate between high and low, designated A and written with a vertical stroke. … Contour tones are extremely rare in Orungu.
tn.cite: Ambouroue, Odette. 2007. Eléments de description de l'orungu, langue bantu du Gabon (B11b). Thèse de doctorat en Philosophie et Lettres (Linguistique), Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB DI-fusion 2013/210699).
tn.note: Three level tones: high, low and downstepped high (a low-high sequence realised after a high); contours very rare; downstep terraces and floating tones; syllable bears tone; few lexical tone pairs.

'Melody on the second syllable' describes the Sherpa tonal contour, not a stress or accent-placement claim for Naawa. 2745.dflt: No positional default is stated. For words in which no syllabic condition gives a simple law ('bisillabi con sillabe brevi e chiuse, trisillabi con sillabe brevi, la 1a e la 3a chiuse, la 2a aperta ecc.') the source says 'influiscono i fattori psicologici: rilievo, unificazione, contrasto e novità producono spostamenti dell'accento' (PT21): such words keep a usual isolation accent that shifts in the phrase (uráy 'volpe' 'viene pronunciata normalmente con l'accento sull'ultima (anche con a semilunga); ma può diventare úray in frasi come: yəmlú șșid n úray'; uššón ~ izún úššən). Vycichl's Kabao informant accepts only tesublá (not tésubla) 'awl', but no rule is stated.
2745.prule: Word accent is determined by syllable weight ('fattori fonetici'): 'Se la sillaba è pesante (presenza di due consonanti o di una vocale lunga), allora si ha l'accento'. For 'a series of words whose accent is constant whatever phrase they occur in': (a) words ending in a doubly closed syllable (C + short V + CC, or C + long V + CC) are accented on that final syllable (tərkóft 'caravan', təbušilt 'girl', tmaharámt 'kerchief'); (b) when the final is short and the penult long, the penult is accented (tmuríut 'hamlet', iməzwárən, imoqránən, ləmdínət 'town'); in Arabic-derived words the Arabic accent tradition may in some cases have had an influence. Where no such syllabic condition gives a simple law ('bisillabi con sillabe brevi e chiuse, trisillabi con sillabe brevi, la 1a e la 3a chiuse, la 2a aperta ecc.'), psychological factors (relief, unification, contrast, novelty) produce accent shifts: a word's usual isolation accent (uráy 'fox', normally final) can retract in the phrase (yəmlú șșid n úray; uššón ~ izún úššən), by Beguinot's law of a final-accented disyllable leaning on a preceding final-accented word 'con qualche possibilità di oscillazione'. Suffixation of demonstratives, possessives etc. changes the syllable structure and with it the accent position; the possessive suffix draws the accent onto itself (udóm ~ udm-ónnəs, ufás ~ ufs-ánnu; mái əlhál-ənnək beside mái əlhal-ónnək). No positional default for words without a heavy syllable is stated.

tn.quote: So far, the data exhibits a considerable number of minimal sets showing the presence of a three-way tonal contrast, High, Mid and Low, in the language. ... Their F0 traces, shown in Figure 1a above, illustrate that they all are level tones ... the tonal contrasts are mostly found on the most prominent syllable, i.e., the stronger syllable, which in this case is the second syllable. The initial syllable or the prefix /ə-/ is weak in the sense that it is not stressed, and hence, it is either toneless or it replicates the tones carried by its corresponding second syllable.
tn.cite: Begum, Asifa. 2023. Champang Phonology. Aligarh Journal of Linguistics 13 (2023-24): 187-206.
tn.locator: sec. 6.1 'Tone minimal sets of Disyllabic roots', pp. 201-202
tn.note: Tentative three level tones (High, Mid, Low) from F0 traces of minimal sets; slight falls called natural; ə- presyllable unstressed, toneless or copies root tone; cites Morey/van Dam doubting tone.
